notes.meaning: Abishur was one of the sons of Shammai in the family line of Jerahmeel. He married Abihail, and together they had two sons named Ahban and Molid. This branch of the family record stops here, likely because their line did not continue further.

Nadab’s family line moved forward through his son Appaim, because his other son Seled died without having any children. The line then passed through Ishi to Sheshan and Ahlai. Ahlai is listed as a child of Sheshan, and commentators explain that Ahlai was either a daughter or a son who died young, since Sheshan had no surviving sons.

Jada was another descendant of Jerahmeel, and his family line continued through his son Jonathan after Jether died childless. Jonathan had two sons named Peleth and Zaza. This note concludes the list of Jerahmeel’s descendants within the larger tribe of Judah.

Sheshan had no sons to carry on his family name and inheritance, only daughters. To keep his family line alive in Israel, he freed his Egyptian servant Jarha, who had likely turned to worship the God of Israel, and gave his daughter to him in marriage. Their son Attai carried on the family line into future generations.

These verses trace the family line begun by the Egyptian servant Jarha and Sheshan's daughter. Generation after generation is recorded, including Zabad, who became one of King David’s mighty warriors. This shows how someone from another nation could become fully included among God's people.

The list of descendants continues through six more generations down to Elishama. This detailed family record spans hundreds of years from Egypt to the later days of the kingdom of Judah. It demonstrates God's faithfulness in preserving this unique family branch among the people of Judah.

The record returns to Caleb, the brother of Jerahmeel and son of Hezron, listing his family lines and town settlements. Being called the father of Ziph and Hebron means these men founded, governed, or populated those cities. In Israel, leaders often cared for their towns like fathers caring for their children.

Hebron's descendants are listed, several of whom share names with well-known southern towns in Judah. Shema and Rekem continued this line, leading to the founders and leaders of places like Jorkeam. These names helped the returning Jewish exiles identify their ancestral lands and towns.

Shammai’s son Maon is identified as the father of Beth-zur. This means Maon either founded or served as the chief leader over the fortified town of Beth-zur in the territory of Judah. The Bible often links family heads directly with the settlements they built and protected.

Caleb also had children by Ephah, a secondary wife who held legal marriage status but fewer inheritance rights than a primary wife. She bore three sons, and the family expanded further down to Gazez. Jahdai's sons are added here as part of these related branches of Caleb's wider family network.

Maacah was another secondary wife of Caleb who bore several sons who became leaders or founders of towns in southern Judah, such as Madmannah and Gibeah. Caleb's daughter Acsah is also highlighted here. She was a woman of note in Judah's history who received an important inheritance of land and springs.

A new branch of Caleb’s descendants is traced through Hur, his firstborn son with Ephrathah. Hur’s sons became the founders and leading rulers of prominent cities in Judah. Among these leaders was Salma, who founded or ruled Bethlehem, the hometown of King David and later the birthplace of Jesus.

Shobal’s descendants settled in and around the town of Kiriath-jearim, dividing into several distinct family groups. These clans later spread out to settle other nearby towns, including Zorah and Eshtaol. Listing these branches helped the returning people of Israel trace their tribal heritage and local rights.

Salma’s descendants populated Bethlehem and surrounding settlements, living alongside families of scribes who worked with legal and religious writings at Jabez. These scribes were Kenites, descendants of Moses's father-in-law's people, who had joined Israel and become fully included in the tribal lands of Judah. Their mention connects them to the faithful Rechabites, known for their devotion to God's ways.
